record.tranche_reason: The author reports their own comparison of features listed for the 1M and 34M SAEs, and an interpretation of activation examples for the Golden Gate Bridge feature. These results qualify the claim that SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units; the post does not test the toy-model superposition claims.
record.gate_note: The post also discusses the source paper's architecture, feature ratios, and neuron correlations; those are commentary or cited results, not separate measurements by this post. Proposed future tests and results reported in the comments are not rows.
record.test_reason: The author's own tally of how many 'More Safety Relevant Features' from Anthropic's 1M SAE have a related counterpart in the 34M SAE bears on whether dictionary features are stable units across dictionaries (V5). The test is weak: it is a manual match against a curated list. The other material is commentary on Anthropic's results, an eyeball re-reading of their diagram, and a null simulation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add a third point: the author argues that Anthropic's reported feature-neuron correlations (~0.3) are much higher than chance. On this view features are more neuron-correlated than Anthropic claims. The author also stresses there is still no gold-standard metric for dictionary quality.
record.recipe_differences: The post comments on another study's SAE results and reports a feature-list comparison and an interpretation of examples; it does not reproduce the original toy-model method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported interpretation of the Golden Gate Bridge feature changes with activation level: the author says the bridge association holds at very high activation but not for the median active instance.

fits_no_version.finding: For the Golden Gate Bridge feature, most active instances (the author estimates ≥90%) are rated irrelevant to the bridge. The label fits only at very high activation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature labels derived from top-activating examples describe only a small high-activation fraction of a feature's activity.

record.problems: The feature recurrence count is based on the author's manual matching of a list, with no stated matching protocol or uncertainty. The Golden Gate activation proportions are explicitly an eyeball estimate rather than a quantitative analysis. No controls or independent validation are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No other results by the post's author met the row criteria. Comments by other users and findings attributed to Anthropic's report were not recorded as this post's own results.

untested.parts: Toy-model superposition, the sparsity transition and the geometry; not addressed.
The capacity account of polysemanticity; not addressed.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure; not addressed.

Whether features are distributed across neurons or recoverable by SAEs. The author only argues, via a null simulation, that Anthropic's reported max feature-neuron correlations (~0.3) exceed chance. No measurement on the model itself.
Completeness, and stability across seeds, models or full dictionaries. Only cross-size recurrence against a curated feature list is checked.
Whether features are one-dimensional; not addressed.

missing.what: The author's null simulation of max correlation between a random feature and ~240K random neurons gives values below 0.02. He argues Anthropic's ~0.3 max feature-neuron correlations are far above chance, so features are more neuron-aligned than Anthropic implies. This bears loosely on V4 (distribution across neurons), but it is a simulated baseline compared against a cited result.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong commentary on Scaling Monosemanticity, which is not an original source here. It contains only one weak own-data test (r1); r2 is a reinterpretation of Anthropic's figure. The V5 verdict is downgraded from challenges to limits_scope because the row state is partial and the matching set is non-exhaustive. Comments by other users are not counted.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, its sparsity-dependent transition, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure explains polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or whether an SAE can recover sparse features; the post uses features reported by another study rather than testing that recoverability.
The post does not establish whether SAE features are complete or stable across other dictionaries, models, or training runs beyond the feature-list comparison it reports.
Whether the represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Compared the listed safety-relevant features in the 1M SAE with the 34M SAE and counted semantically related matches.
rows.measure: Recurrence of listed 1M SAE features in related form in the 34M SAE
rows.locator: Finding Specific Features; table of 1M and 34M safety-relevant features
rows.note: The author says this tally is their own count and interprets it as evidence that the approach does not find a consistent set of features. This is a comparison of feature lists, not an evaluation across training seeds.
rows.check: Linking and state are right: 7/22 features recur and 15/22 do not. Matching was manual, with no protocol, and was done against Anthropic's curated 34M list rather than the full dictionary. A commenter notes the list is not exhaustive, so non-recurrence may be overstated.

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Eyeballed the distribution of activations and relevance examples for the Golden Gate Bridge feature.

conditions.value: median active instance versus very high activation

rows.measure: Share of active instances the author regards as irrelevant versus relevant to the Golden Gate Bridge
rows.value: At least 90/10 between the left mass and right mass; the author says the split might be 99/1. At the median active instance, the feature is described as irrelevant to the Golden Gate Bridge.
rows.locator: A Feature Isn't Its Highest Activating Examples; annotated Anthropic diagram and linked feature page
rows.note: The proportions are the author's eyeballing of the source diagram, not a reported quantitative evaluation. The author says the feature corresponds to the bridge at very high activation.
rows.check: This measures how well a feature's label describes its low-activation instances (interpretability/specificity). It does not measure whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units, so it bears on no version. The '90/10, maybe 99/1' split is the author's eyeballing of Anthropic's own diagram and autointerp scores, not a new measurement. Moved to fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Claude 3 Sonnet SAEs, 1M vs 34M, curated safety-relevant feature list
relationships.reason: Only 7/22 listed 1M features have a related 34M counterpart, so features are not consistently recovered across dictionary sizes. The test is a manual match against a non-exhaustive list (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Only 7 of 22 listed 1M features had a related 34M counterpart, based on manual matching against a non-exhaustive list.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
